::: {.cite-bar .domain-intelligence}
[Superseded]{.status .status-superseded} [Pub. L. 93-559]{.cite} [88 Stat. 1795]{.cite} [formerly 22 U.S.C. 2422]{.cite}
:::

Section 32 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1974, which added section 662 to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. It barred spending on CIA operations abroad other than intelligence collection unless the President found the operation important to national security and reported it to Congress.

## Key provisions

- Required a presidential finding for each covert operation.
- Required a timely report to the appropriate committees, which at the time meant as many as eight.

## Why it matters

It ended plausible presidential deniability for covert action and was the first statute to require notice to Congress. The [Intel Oversight Act](intel-oversight-1980.qmd) narrowed the reporting to the two intelligence committees and the 1991 intelligence authorization act replaced it outright.

## Current status

Repealed in 1991 and replaced by the covert action provisions now at 50 U.S.C. 3093.
